background_notes.fact: A metric set of finite extended diameter is bounded, its real diameter is nonnegative and bounds every pairwise distance, and coordinate projections from MaxProd(X) do not increase diameter. For a nonempty real set B with all |b-b'|≤r<∞, its real infimum l and supremum u exist and satisfy B⊆[l,u] and 0≤u-l≤r.

Extended diameter is the supremum of pairwise extended distances.
Real diameter agrees with extended diameter on bounded sets.

background_notes.justification: For a nonempty set fix a member; the pairwise bound places every other member in a ball of finite radius. Coordinate distances are bounded by the maximum product distance, so their suprema are bounded by the same diameter. For nonempty B choose b0∈B; B lies in [b0-r,b0+r], so real completeness supplies l,u. For each b'∈B, every b∈B satisfies b≤b'+r; taking the supremum gives u-r≤b'. This is a lower bound for B, hence u-r≤l. Nonemptiness gives l≤u. Empty sets are handled separately as in S001.

background_notes.fact: Closed real intervals and the empty set are Borel measurable, finite intersections of measurable sets are measurable, and a measure satisfies μ(∅)=0 and μ(S)≤μ(T) whenever S⊆T.

background_notes.justification: The complement of a closed interval is a union of open rays, so the interval is Borel. Sigma-algebras contain the empty set and are closed under complements and finite unions, hence finite intersections. Measure monotonicity follows by writing a measurable superset as a disjoint union with its measurable difference and using nonnegative additivity. The applications here involve Borel sets I∩J_i and J_i.

background_notes.fact: Nonnegative extended multiplication and nonnegative series preserve inequalities. For finite r≥0 and s>0, casting nonnegative real powers into ℝ≥0∞ preserves products and order, and r^s·r=r^(s+1), including r=0.

background_notes.justification: Extended nonnegative multiplication is order preserving, with the defined zero-times-infinity value zero. A nonnegative series is the supremum of its finite subsums, so finite termwise comparisons imply the comparison of series, without convergence assumptions. For r>0 the power identity follows from exp((s+1)log r)=exp(s log r)exp(log r); for r=0 both exponents are positive, so both sides are zero. The embedding of finite nonnegative reals into ℝ≥0∞ preserves these operations. Thus the displayed estimate remains valid even when c or a series is infinite.
